title: A For Rent Sign in New Brunswick and Dressings No One Could Inspect
dek: In 1886 three Johnson brothers rented one floor of an old wallpaper factory to make surgical dressings for a method many surgeons still doubted.

story.founder: Robert Wood Johnson, James Wood Johnson and Edward Mead Johnson
story.event: Founding a factory in New Brunswick to make ready-made antiseptic surgical dressings, and teaching doctors the method
story.summary: In January 1886 James Wood Johnson rented the top floor of a former wallpaper factory in New Brunswick, New Jersey, where he and his brother Edward Mead Johnson, joined that September by their brother Robert Wood Johnson, began making ready-made surgical dressings for Lister's antiseptic surgery with 14 employees. Because their quality could not be seen, the firm stressed cleanliness and labelling, and in 1888 published a free manual, Modern Methods of Antiseptic Wound Treatment, to teach doctors the method. Heat sterilisation on an industrial scale followed around 1890-91.
paragraphs: In January 1886, James Wood Johnson was on a Pennsylvania Railroad train from New York towards Philadelphia when it stopped at New Brunswick, New Jersey. From the window he saw a four-storey red-brick building with a For Rent sign: the old Janeway & Carpender wallpaper factory. He got off, looked it over, and rented the top floor.

He and his brother Edward Mead Johnson had left Seabury & Johnson, the firm their elder brother Robert had co-founded, to make ready-made surgical dressings for antiseptic surgery. Robert, who by the company's account had heard Joseph Lister describe the method in Philadelphia in 1876, was still bound by the agreement that dissolved the old firm, and joined them that September. They were betting on medicine that was not yet settled. Many doctors found it hard to believe that invisible germs caused the infections that so often followed operations, and those who wanted to try Lister's methods often lacked the materials and the know-how.

The brothers started with 14 employees, eight women and six men, though a local paper had forecast 50 to 100. Their product could not be judged by eye: a dressing that looked clean might not be. Workers were expected to keep their hands and surroundings clean, and each package carried directions for keeping its contents free of germs. Then the company set out to teach the method itself. In 1888 it published Modern Methods of Antiseptic Wound Treatment, compiled from leading surgeons' notes, for doctors without operating theatres. "The ordinary kitchen table will generally answer," it advised, with a soup tureen for rinsed sponges and saucers for needles. Within months, the company says, 85,000 copies had gone out free to doctors and pharmacists.

The first dressings were antiseptic, prepared with germicides such as carbolic acid and iodoform. True sterilisation by heat came soon after: by 1890, by one account, the company was using dry heat, and in 1891 it began steam sterilisation on an industrial scale. Fred Kilmer, the New Brunswick pharmacist who had led work on the manual, became scientific director and set up an Aseptic Department of clean rooms. The company kept its headquarters in the town where James stepped off the train.

quote.text: is it possible to be free from faults (if you do all this)? It is not possible; but this is possible, to direct your efforts incessantly to being faultless. For we must be content if by never remitting this attention we shall escape at least a few errors.
quote.source_title: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus with the Encheiridion, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #10661
quote.connection: Epictetus promises no freedom from faults, only attention that does not lapse and so catches a few more errors. The brothers could not see a germ on a dressing, so they built habits around it instead: clean hands, clean rooms, careful labels and a book of method.

reflection: The brothers' product had an awkward property: its quality could not be seen. A clean-looking dressing might carry exactly what it was meant to keep out. So the work moved to everything around the product, from washed hands to printed directions to a free book teaching doctors how to use it. Customers could not inspect the quality, so the company had to make it trustworthy.

Laboratory results share that property, and much of what talQen is for lives in the same place: the routine checks and records that make an invisible standard visible. Epictetus does not ask for a faultless day, only steady attention that catches a few more errors. That is a standard a tired person can still keep.
invitation: Choose one routine check you do every day almost without thinking. Do it once today with your full attention, and note one small thing you had stopped noticing.

cross_checks.claim: The three Johnson brothers began making surgical dressings in 1886 in a former wallpaper factory in New Brunswick, New Jersey, with 14 employees
The company was founded to make products for Lister's antiseptic surgery, which inspired Robert Wood Johnson
In 1888 the company published Modern Methods of Antiseptic Wound Treatment, advising that an ordinary kitchen table would serve for an operation
Heat sterilisation on an industrial scale followed around 1890-91

research_notes: Founding: the company's chief historian (2016) says James and Edward Mead Johnson started the business in early 1886 and Robert joined only in September 1886, when the agreement dissolving Seabury & Johnson allowed; other company pages and the International Directory of Company Histories say the three brothers founded it in 1886. Grace's Guide (not cited, page would not load for the verifier) and a 2000 newspaper item give 1885; the brothers left Seabury & Johnson in 1885, which may explain it. The story uses January 1886 for the rented floor and September 1886 for Robert. Lister: the company says Robert heard Lister in Philadelphia in 1876; a pharmaphorum piece (not cited) says 1885; a blog notes there is no ticket or diary proving his attendance, so the story says 'by the company's account'. 'Sterile': company pages call the 1886-87 products sterile, but the 1888 manual itself describes moist antiseptic gauzes (bichloride, iodoform, carbolated) alongside heat-sterilised cotton; the International Directory says dry-heat sterilisation of bandages came by 1890, and the company timeline dates industrial steam sterilisation to 1891. The story therefore calls the first dressings antiseptic and dates heat sterilisation to 1890-91, giving the dry-heat date as one account. Kilmer: joined in 1888 by the International Directory, 1889 by the company timeline and 'about a year' after the manual project by Our Beginning; the story gives no year. First product: the International Directory says it was an improved medicinal plaster; company pages say surgical supplies; the story avoids naming a first product. Copies: 85,000 within months is the company's figure (two company pages agree); no independent figure found, so it is attributed. The manual was published from Johnson & Johnson's New York sales office (25 Cedar Street) and is undated; the Wellcome Collection's catalogue notes its latest internal date is February 1888. Funding: no outside investors are recorded; marked bootstrapped. Epictetus's chapter is about moral attention; it is applied by analogy to working attention. This is the one edition in my group that mentions talQen.
